hero.title: Is AI Audio in Real-Time Possible in Games?
hero.subtitle: Graduate research: can AI generate game audio fast enough for real-time playback?

section1.title: What's This Project About?
section1.intro: You might be wondering why anyone would even try to generate sounds with AI in games. Well, it's actually a pretty cool question - what if instead of having hundreds of pre-recorded sound effects, games could create them on the fly? Sounds like science fiction, right?
section1.testing: So for the past few weeks, I've been testing exactly that. The main question was:
section1.question: Is AI fast enough that players wouldn't even notice the delay between an action and its sound?
section1.findings: The direct answer so far: AI is too slow for instant playback. BUT - I'm exploring a workaround to use AI quality in games. How? Keep reading.

section2.title: Making Unity and Python Talk
section2.intro: At first, I had to figure out the basics - connecting Unity with Python through WebSocket. Sounds complicated, but in practice Unity just says "hey Python, give me a gunshot sound", and Python generates it and sends it back.
section2.results_intro: First tests with a simple procedural generator looked promising:
section2.results_note: Sounds great! Everything under 60ms is practically unnoticeable to players. The only problem was that these sounds, well... sounded synthetic. Like something from a 90s game. I needed something better.

section3.title: The 12-Second Nightmare
section3.intro: I expected latency. I didn't expect this.
section3.failure_context: Time to generate one footstep with AudioLDM.
section3.narrative: In a game running at 60 FPS, a footstep needs to happen in 16 milliseconds. My first attempt was 750 times too slow. Even the faster MusicGen model took 4 seconds. In the world of game development, 4 seconds is an eternity. It was a complete failure.

section4.title: The 0.03ms Anomaly
section4.intro: I was ready to scrap the project. But then, during a frustration-filled debug session, I noticed something weird in the logs.
section4.epiphany: The second time I requested the same sound, it didn't generate it. It pulled it from memory. It was instant. Faster than any hard drive reading a WAV file.
section4.question: We don't need to be fast. We just need to be early.

section5.title: Predictive Generation
section5.intro: If we can't generate sound in real-time, we have to generate it before it happens. This shifted the entire architecture from 'Reaction' to 'Prediction'.
section5.explanation: I built a system that uses the loading screen—a place where players expect to wait—to 'hallucinate' the audio for the level ahead. By the time the player spawns, the AI has already done the heavy lifting. The result? Zero latency. High-fidelity AI audio.

section6.title: The New Problem: Memory vs. Chaos
section6.intro: So we solved the speed limit by 'cheating' with the loading screen. But this victory created a new, more dangerous enemy: RAM Usage.
section6.problem: If we pre-generate every possible sound for an open-world game, we would need terabytes of RAM. We traded CPU time for Memory, and now we're running out of space.
section6.current_work: This is where my research is right now. I am moving away from 'Pre-generate Everything' to something smarter: Predictive Buffering.

section7.title: Active Experiments
section7.intro: I am currently running three parallel experiments to solve the memory crisis:
section7.exp1_desc: Deleting sounds immediately after they are played to free up RAM.
section7.exp2_desc: AI that guesses what you will do in the next 10 seconds and generates ONLY that.
section7.status_desc: The '0.03ms Cache' works, but making it scalable is the new frontier. I am currently coding the prediction algorithm in Python.

section8.title: Update: Verification (06 Dec 2025)
section8.intro: The '0.03ms Anomaly' wasn't a glitch. It was the answer. I spent the weekend stress-testing this new 'Hybrid' approach against the old 'Pure AI' method.
section8.session2_desc: I gave the local models one last chance on standard hardware. It's confirmed useless. 4-10 seconds of silence for a single footstep. We can't ship that.
section8.session4_desc: This actually works. The procedural engine handles the immediate feedback (<5ms), while the AI generates the high-fidelity asset in the background. To the player, it just feels instant.
section8.stats_intro: Final metrics from the stress test:
section8.summary: We aren't just cheating time anymore. We're managing it. The system is stable.
